Please read this carefully:

<document>
# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

</document>
response:
This paper is much stronger than the previous one. It is a registered, stratified, cluster-randomised design. It uses administrative output, measures actual hours, and labels its exploratory analysis honestly. It also directly answers the "sector-general" claim with the right distinction: whether output depends on staff being present. The arithmetic is consistent:
- Case-processing: 0.979 / 0.87 ≈ +12.5% per actual hour, and 0.979 / 0.8 ≈ +22% per scheduled hour.
- Counter offices: 0.886 / 0.83 ≈ +6.7% per actual hour.
- The hours changes match the timesheet figures.

The main conclusions are broadly supported. The problems below are about precision and interpretation, not a reversal of the findings.

## 1. Too few clusters for standard clustered standard errors

The strata have 14 offices (7 v 7) and 10 offices (5 v 5). Conventional cluster-robust standard errors are known to be too small with this few clusters, so the confidence intervals are probably too narrow. This matters most for:
- the counter stratum's output-per-hour interval (+0.4 to +13.3), which is near zero;
- the sick-day and resignation estimates.

The paper should use small-cluster methods, such as a wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference over the actual assignment.

## 2. The sick-day reduction may be partly built into the measure

The paper doesn't say how the 30-hour week was arranged. If treated staff work four days instead of five, a week of illness records as 4 sick days instead of 5. Sick days per FTE would then fall about 20% even if illness didn't change at all, which would account for much of the reported −29%.

The paper should:
- state the rota pattern;
- report sickness absence as a share of scheduled hours;
- give a confidence interval, since the −29% currently has none;
- explain why this one outcome is pooled across strata when everything else is stratified.

## 3. The per-hour gain in counter offices may just be busier staff, paid for by the public

With unchanged opening hours and fewer staff on duty, queues lengthen and staff have less idle time between contacts. Contacts per hour worked rise for that reason, not because staff work more effectively. The rise in waiting times is the visible sign of this.

So "each hour worked was somewhat more productive" is better read as "each hour worked was more fully used, at the cost of the public's time." The paper's broader conclusion, that the change didn't pay for itself in this work, holds either way. But the +6.7% shouldn't be presented as evidence that rest improves productivity.

The size of the output fall also needs explaining:
- Rising call abandonment (6% → 10%) accounts for only about 4 percentage points of the 11.4% fall in contacts handled.
- A breakdown is needed: in-person walk-aways, changes in demand, and the telephone and counter channels separately.
- Repeat contacts count as output, so the higher repeat-contact rate in treated offices slightly flatters the output figure.

## 4. The contrast between strata isn't formally tested, and one comparison is overstated

- **Output per employee** (−2.1% v −11.4%): this difference is probably real. A rough calculation gives z ≈ 2.5. Still, the paper should report the interaction test, and say whether it was part of the registered plan.
- **Output per hour** (+12.5% v +6.7%): the confidence intervals overlap almost entirely, so this difference is not established. Calling the counter figure "a more modest 6.7%" in the Summary implies a difference the data can't support.

## 5. Several outcomes are reported without control comparisons or intervals

The paper's analysis is difference-in-differences, but several outcomes don't follow it:
- **Waiting time** (4.2 → 6.9 minutes) and **abandoned calls** (6% → 10%) are given for treated offices only, before and after, with no control trend. Seasonal or demand changes can't be ruled out.
- **Quality measures** (3.1% v 3.0%; 11.8% v 10.9%) are given as levels with no confidence interval. They also don't say whether these are treated-versus-control or before-versus-after.
- **Appeal overturns** take time to appear. Decisions made in the last months of the trial may not have been appealed yet, so nine months may undercount quality problems.

## 6. Hours, overtime and cost

- **Unrecorded hours:** timesheets capture claimed overtime only. If staff also worked unclaimed time, actual hours are understated and the per-hour gain is overstated. This is the same problem the paper rightly criticises in other studies, in milder form.
- **Overtime pay:** case-processing staff kept full pay *and* claimed overtime, likely at a premium rate.
- **Missing cost measure:** the county's stated question was whether the schedule could be extended "without loss of service." Cost per case, or cost per contact, is the natural measure for that question and isn't reported. Neutral output per employee alongside higher pay costs is a different result from neutral output alone.

## 7. Backlog and case mix

"Cases closed" can be held up by clearing easy cases first, leaving the backlog older and more complex. The Limitations section raises the risk of backlogs building past statutory deadlines but defers it to the follow-up. The case-management system should already hold:
- backlog size and age;
- the share of cases meeting statutory deadlines;
- case-mix weights.

These could be reported at nine months.

## 8. The "per FTE" denominator is ambiguous

If FTE is measured against 37.5 hours, a treated employee on 30 hours would count as 0.8 FTE, and output per FTE would *rise*. The text uses "per FTE" and "per employee" interchangeably, which suggests the denominator is headcount. The paper should say so explicitly.

## 9. The meetings analysis is weaker than its caveats suggest

The paper is appropriately cautious, but a few points go further than its stated caveats:
- **No pre-period data:** meetings were recorded in month six only. The 3.8 v 7.1 hour gap could partly predate the trial, so it can't be shown to be a *reduction*.
- **Very wide uncertainty:** with only 7 offices, a correlation of r = 0.71 has a 95% interval running from roughly zero to about 0.95.
- **Implied size, if confirmed:** suppose meeting time sits inside timesheet hours and pre-trial meeting levels were similar across arms. Then non-meeting hours were about 29.2 (treated) against 30.8 (control), only about 5% lower. Output per non-meeting hour would be up only about 3%, meaning meetings could account for most of the case-processing per-hour gain, not just "part" of it. The follow-up's confirmatory test should be designed with this possibility in mind.

## 10. Smaller points

- **"Little or no measurable loss"** in case-processing: the confidence interval extends to −6.8%, so a moderate loss isn't excluded. "No statistically detectable loss; losses up to about 7% cannot be ruled out" would be more accurate.
- **Missing figure:** the scheduled-hours comparison for counter offices (about +11%) should be reported next to the case-processing 22%. This would complete the third conclusion about overstatement.
- **Control-group effects:** the Limitations note that control staff knew about the trial, but not the specific risk of resentment in control offices. That could raise their resignations and sickness, inflating the treatment–control gaps. If county transfer records exist, check whether staff moved between offices during the trial.
- **Missing interval in the Summary:** the Summary gives output per actual hour without a confidence interval, unlike the other headline figures.

## Overall

The core findings stand:
- Hours cuts are roughly output-neutral per employee in backlog-based work.
- They are clearly costly in work that depends on staff being present.
- Measuring against scheduled hours overstates gains substantially.

The revisions that would most strengthen the paper are:
- small-cluster inference;
- a sickness measure that isn't built into the schedule change;
- difference-in-differences estimates with intervals for waiting time, abandonment and quality;
- cost per unit of output;
- backlog and case-mix data;
- a more cautious reading of the per-hour gain in counter offices.

If you'd like, I can draft a referee report from these points, or a short comparison of this paper with the 61-organisation pilot.
